title: Why most ML/AI trading models collapse in live execution (and 6 real strategy rules)
author: Yoksel_algo
selftext:
​

When newcomers ask about algo trading or machine learning setups, it’s usually the same few questions: \*"What’s the best strategy?"\*, \*"Which indicators actually work?"\*, or \*"What timeframe should I use?"\*

That entire line of thinking skips the actual hard part. Survival in real markets comes down to system mechanics, hard risk boundaries, and execution logic—not finding a fancy visual pattern on a chart.

Here is how we restructure strategy engineering, and what backtesters are actually supposed to do.

\---

\### 6 Core Strategy Rules

Before writing code or training models, these rules need to be hardcoded into the strategy logic:

1. \*\*Explicit Risk Spectrum:\*\* A strategy is defined strictly by the drawdown and tail-risk you’re willing to take. If you can't quantify your worst-case drawdown boundary, you don't have a strategy—you have a wish.

2. \*\*Minimize Risk First, Yield Second:\*\* The job of a quant model isn't to chase peak returns. It’s to cap drawdowns and control risk capacity. Position sizing, leverage limits, and asset picks are built \*around\* risk containment. Profit is just a byproduct of surviving.

3. \*\*Know the Math Behind Every Feature:\*\* Indicators aren't buy/sell signals. They’re mathematical transforms designed to isolate specific dynamics (momentum, mean-reversion, volatility compression). If you can't break down what the math is doing to the raw price data, don't use it as a feature.

4. \*\*No Random Indicator Stacking:\*\* Throwing 15 indicators into a pipeline hoping the model "figures it out" just feeds it noise. You need a clear rationale for how every tool interacts with the others. If you can’t explain why two metrics belong together, keep them out.

5. \*\*AI Is an Analyst, Not the Decision-Maker:\*\* Use ML to process features, catch statistical anomalies, or dynamically estimate risk metrics. Never hand it the keys to trade execution.

6. \*\*Hard Guardrails Over Black Boxes:\*\* Never build a setup where entry and exit execution relies solely on unconstrained neural net output. Without deterministic, rule-based execution bounds, the model \*will\* hit a regime shift and wipe out the balance.

\---

\### Backtesters Don't Predict—They Stress-Test

People misuse backtesters all the time. A backtest shouldn't be used to estimate future profits; it’s a friction filter to see if the logic survives real execution.

And while a poorly built standard backtester can distort reality, \*\*an ML model with look-ahead data leakage lies every single time.\*\*

\#### Fixing the Optimism Bias

If your features accidentally pull data from future bars, or your engine assumes instant fills at $Mid$ price, the backtest is worthless fiction.

\* \*\*The Look-Ahead Trap:\*\* Supervised ML models love to cheat. Incorrect normalization, overlapping features, or standard K-Fold splitting quietly leak future target data into current training samples. That paper-traded 92% win rate is almost always just target leakage.

\* \*\*Pessimistic Intra-Bar Fills:\*\* Backtesters must enforce worst-case outcomes. If you're running 1-minute bars and a Take-Profit and Stop-Loss (or adverse slippage) trigger inside the \*same\* bar, your engine \*\*must assume the bad outcome happened first\*\*. No exceptions.

\* \*\*The Real Benchmark:\*\* A valid backtest doesn't guarantee live profit. It just proves your edge can outlive slippage, spreads, and queue delays. If a model stays positive under deliberately hostile fill assumptions, it earned a shot on live data.

\---

\### Discussion for Developers

To the ML engineers, quants, and developers here:

1. \*\*Indicator Efficiency:\*\* In your feature pipelines, which specific technical indicators or mathematical transforms give you the highest signal-to-noise ratio? 

2. \*\*TA Features vs. Raw Microstructure:\*\* What yields better predictive power in your setups—engineered TA features (RSI, ATR, volatility regimes) or raw market microstructure (order book depth, trade flow, fractional differentiation)?

Curious to hear what actually made it into your production engines.

replies.author: Yoksel_algo
replies.body:
Bravo - you already know the single most important rule here and you're actually applying it.
Running proper backtests + stress tests before deploying anything is basic risk hygiene. If you can't map out worst-case scenarios and friction for a specific asset ahead of time, you're just gambling with leverage. 
And honestly, you're not alone on the indicator side. Most devs just drop 10 tools on a chart without looking at the underlying math, then wonder why their feature pipeline is full of redundant noise or signal conflicts. 
Moving averages, Stochastics, MACD, divergence models... none of them are inherently bad. But the indicator combo itself doesn't give you an edge. What actually matters is the post-friction statistical output: your expected payoff, max drawdown boundary, and tail risk containment. 
Bottom line though: never put an indicator in your setup if you don't fully understand its logic and inner mechanics. If you can't break down its exact transform on raw price data, keep it out. Clean logic you completely control will beat a complex pipeline of black boxes every single time.
Wish you the best of luck with the build—keep putting in the hours, stay disciplined, and don't stop.
